excerpts.title: Beauty Holiday Sale - Post-campaign review
excerpts.content:
Post-campaign review | Beauty | Beauty Holiday Sale | 2025-12-04 | Host: Derek Wright
Beauty Holiday Sale - Post-Campaign Review > What Worked

- GMV reached $843.5K, within the $800K-$1,090K target range.
- Conversion rate was 7.78%, within the 7%-9% target range.
- Operating cost was $139.0K against planned $143.2K, 2.9% under budget.
- Lipstick delivered $119.6K in profit on $230.3K in sales, with a 51.92% margin.

excerpts.title: Beauty Black Friday Live - Post-campaign review
heading_path: Beauty Black Friday Live - Post-Campaign Review
ROI (the formula changed; here is why)
excerpts.content:
Post-campaign review | Beauty | Beauty Black Friday Live | 2025-11-18 | Host: Tommy Walter
Beauty Black Friday Live - Post-Campaign Review > ROI (the formula changed; here is why)

The first two versions were wrong. The first one subtracted only the operating cost, not the product cost, so ROI looked too high. The second one added the product cost to the denominator, which is also wrong: product cost is already deducted in campaign_products.profit (profit = sales - product cost; the customer pays for the goods, it is not money the company spent on this campaign). The real question is: how much profit did the marketing spend (the operating cost) bring in?

- Total product profit (sum of profit over the 3 featured products in campaign_products, product cost already deducted): $168.8K
- Actual operating cost (campaigns.actual_operating_cost): $73.6K
- ROI = total product profit / operating cost = 168.8 / 73.6 ≈ 2.29: every $1 of marketing spend brought back about $2.29 of product profit

Both numbers now come from structured fields (SUM(campaign_products.profit) and campaigns.actual_operating_cost), so the review no longer estimates them by hand or improvises a formula.

SOP | All departments
Refund and Return Requests > Procedure

1. Check the item and request. a. Confirm the delivery date and whether the item is within the 30-day return window. Customers can return an item within 30 days of delivery. b. excerpts.title: Livestream Incident Response
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Livestream Incident Response > Purpose

This procedure applies company-wide to livestream incidents, including stream interruptions, pricing errors, product sellouts, and offensive comments. The Live Operations team owns this procedure.

excerpts.title: Livestream Incident Response
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Livestream Incident Response > Procedure

1. Respond to a dropped stream. a. The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes of the stream dropping. b. While the producer switches streams, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update.
2. Respond to a wrong price on screen. a. Remove the product link at once. b. Review orders placed at the wrong price. Honor orders if the error is less than 30% off the right price. Otherwise, cancel the orders and provide an apology coupon of $10. c. The host should give a brief, accurate update and avoid confirming an order outcome before it is reviewed.
3. Respond to a product that sells out mid-stream. a. The host announces that the product has sold out and moves to the next product. b. Do not promise a waitlist on air.
4. Respond to a raid of offensive comments. a. The moderator turns on slow mode and blocks the accounts posting offensive comments. b. The host does not respond to the comments and continues the stream.
5. Document and follow up. a. The responsible Live Operations staff member files the incident log within 1 hour after the stream ends. b. Send a short post-incident note the next day. Include a concise summary of what happened and the actions taken.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

1. Check that frozen items are packed with dry ice and scheduled to spend at most 48 hours in transit.
2. Do not ship frozen items on Fridays; this avoids weekend depot delays.
3. If a customer reports spoilage, request a claim within 24 hours of delivery and ask for a photo.
4. Offer the customer a choice between a refund and a new shipment.
5. If claims exceed 3% of a shipment, review the carrier.

Keep the claim process straightforward. Use the delivery time to determine whether the claim was made within 24 hours, and make sure the photo is attached to the claim record. The photo helps the team understand the reported condition instead of relying only on a description. Record the customer’s chosen resolution and route the case through the normal fulfillment process.

The shipping rules are preventive controls, not a guarantee that spoilage cannot occur. Dry ice supports frozen products during transit, while the transit limit and Friday restriction reduce exposure to delays. If a shipment misses its expected timing or arrives with a problem, handle the customer’s report under the claim process rather than assuming the packaging controls were sufficient.

Review the carrier when claims exceed 3% of a shipment. Look at the shipment’s claim records and available delivery information to understand whether carrier handling or delays may have contributed. Escalate the review through the Fresh Grocery Logistics team so the carrier issue can be considered and followed up.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > Purpose

Owner: Fresh Grocery Logistics team. Category: Fulfillment.

Fresh grocery can spoil if it is exposed to warm conditions or delayed in transit. This procedure sets clear shipping and claim rules so customers receive safe products and the team can respond consistently when a shipment arrives spoiled. Frozen items ship with dry ice and spend at most 48 hours in transit. They do not ship on Fridays, which prevents them from sitting in a depot over the weekend. These limits reduce the time frozen products are exposed to conditions that could compromise them. When spoilage occurs despite these controls, a timely claim with a photo gives the team useful evidence to assess the issue and address the customer’s needs. The customer chooses between a refund and a new shipment. The team also reviews carrier performance when claims exceed 3% of a shipment, so recurring problems can be identified and addressed. Follow the steps below for every relevant shipment and spoilage claim.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > Common Mistakes

Do not schedule frozen items to ship on Fridays. A shipment can then remain at a depot over the weekend, increasing the risk of spoilage.

Do not omit dry ice or allow frozen items to spend more than 48 hours in transit.

Do not treat a spoilage report as a complete claim without a photo, or overlook the requirement that the claim be made within 24 hours of delivery.

Do not choose the resolution for the customer. The customer decides between a refund and a new shipment.

Do not ignore the carrier review threshold. When claims exceed 3% of a shipment, start a carrier review.

excerpts.title: Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

Check the product and its supporting information before the livestream introduction. Confirm that the on-screen details match the product being sold, including allergen information, origin details where required, and any organic claim. For shipment, check the best-before date on the food itself. These checks cover separate risks: a correct on-screen description does not confirm the date on the stock that will ship, and a suitable date does not make an incomplete product description acceptable. If a required detail is missing, unclear, or unsupported, pause the introduction or shipment until the Fresh Grocery Quality team has advised what to do.

1. Confirm allergens are shown on screen when the product is introduced.
2. Check the best-before date on the product selected for shipment.
3. Confirm country of origin for meat and seafood, and verify the certificate number for any organic claim.
4. Hold the item if a check fails, and ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team for guidance.

Allergens such as nuts and shellfish must be shown on screen when the product is introduced. Customers may need this information before deciding whether to buy, so the relevant allergen details should be visible at the point the product is presented, not left for customers to infer from the product name or a later discussion. Check that the on-screen information corresponds to the item being introduced. If the details are missing or do not match the product, do not proceed with the introduction until the information has been checked and corrected.

For chilled food, the product must have at least 10 days left before its best-before date when it ships. For dry goods, it must have at least 90 days left before its best-before date when it ships. Check the date on the actual product selected for the order, since stock may have different dates even when it is the same item. If the product does not meet the applicable requirement, do not ship it. Ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team to confirm the next step.

The country of origin must be stated for meat and seafood. Any organic claim must include the certificate number. Confirm that these details are available and apply to the product being sold; do not add an origin or organic statement based on assumption alone.

answer: Send the complete script and all planned product visuals, including product pictures, to the Beauty Compliance team 3 business days before the stream. [1]

excerpts.title: Product Claims and Compliance Review (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Product Claims and Compliance Review (Beauty) > How It Works

The script must be reviewed 3 business days before the stream. Send the complete script and any planned product visuals to the Beauty Compliance team, including claims, demonstrations, before-and-after photos, and on-screen product information. Review the full presentation rather than only isolated phrases: a combination of spoken wording, visuals, and product details can imply a claim that is not stated outright. If the team identifies an issue, update the script or materials and return them for review before the stream. Do not assume that a claim is acceptable because it appears in brand copy or has been used in another stream; the current product and supporting materials must be checked.

Core steps:

1. Submit the script and planned visuals for review 3 business days before the stream.
2. Resolve review comments and confirm the final version with the Beauty Compliance team.
3. Use only the approved script and materials during the stream.

Scripts must not say “cures”, “medical grade”, “guaranteed anti-aging” or “100% natural” unless the product is certified. These terms can imply medical effects, a guarantee, or a specific standard, so do not include them based on informal assurances or general product descriptions. If the product is certified, provide the relevant support to the reviewer and use the wording only as approved. An SPF claim needs the product’s test report; do not make or display the claim until that report has been provided and reviewed. Evidence should support the product being sold, not merely a similar item or a general ingredient claim.

Before-and-after photos need the brand’s written consent and must not be retouched. Consent helps confirm that the brand has approved the images for use, while unretouched photos reduce the risk of presenting an altered result as typical or genuine. When a skincare product is introduced, its ingredient list stays on screen for 10 seconds. Keep the list readable and visible for the full display period so customers have a fair chance to review what the product contains.

Product Claims and Compliance Review (Beauty) > Common Mistakes

A common mistake is treating a phrase as acceptable because it is familiar in beauty sales. The wording still needs certification or evidence where required. Another is using an SPF claim before the test report has been reviewed, or using before-and-after photos without written consent. Do not retouch photos to improve how a result looks. Do not remove the ingredient list too quickly or cover it with other graphics during the required display.

excerpts.title: Product Claims and Compliance Review (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Product Claims and Compliance Review (Beauty) > Purpose

Owner: Beauty Compliance team. Category: Compliance.

This procedure sets out how Beauty reviews product claims and presentation before a livestream. Customers rely on what hosts say and show when deciding whether a product is right for them, so claims must be accurate, supportable, and consistent with the product information the brand has approved. A claim that sounds stronger than the available evidence can mislead customers and create compliance risk for the company and the brand. Review also covers visual material and the way product details appear during the stream, because photos and on-screen information can communicate claims just as directly as spoken words. The review gives the team time to identify unsupported wording, request evidence or consent, and correct the script before it is used. Hosts and producers should treat approval as part of stream preparation, not as a final check after the show is ready.

excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Sale Event Inventory Check (Fresh Grocery) > Procedure

1. Forecast demand: Estimate expected sales from the GMV and DAU of similar past campaigns and the promotion's expected reach.
2. Confirm supplier capacity: Seven days ahead, confirm with suppliers that their capacity covers the forecast; for fresh products, also confirm cold-chain shipping capacity.
3. Check shelf life: Every product on sale must stay within its shelf life until at least three days after the campaign ends, to avoid complaints about near-expiry goods.
4. Sync the inventory system: Reserve the campaign stock in the system so other channels cannot oversell it and livestream orders never hit an empty shelf.
5. Prepare warehouse and cold chain: For fresh products, confirm cold-storage capacity and that shipping times can handle the order spike during the sale.
6. Plan for problem SKUs: If a SKU's stock looks wrong after the campaign starts (far above or below forecast), decide who pulls it or restocks it, and how fast they must respond.
7. Count after the campaign: Compare actual shipments with the system's stock records; investigate large differences (see the post-livestream review process).

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

1. Check that frozen items are packed with dry ice and scheduled to spend at most 48 hours in transit.
2. Do not ship frozen items on Fridays; this avoids weekend depot delays.
3. If a customer reports spoilage, request a claim within 24 hours of delivery and ask for a photo.
4. Offer the customer a choice between a refund and a new shipment.
5. If claims exceed 3% of a shipment, review the carrier.

Keep the claim process straightforward. Use the delivery time to determine whether the claim was made within 24 hours, and make sure the photo is attached to the claim record. The photo helps the team understand the reported condition instead of relying only on a description. Record the customer’s chosen resolution and route the case through the normal fulfillment process.

The shipping rules are preventive controls, not a guarantee that spoilage cannot occur. Dry ice supports frozen products during transit, while the transit limit and Friday restriction reduce exposure to delays. If a shipment misses its expected timing or arrives with a problem, handle the customer’s report under the claim process rather than assuming the packaging controls were sufficient.

Review the carrier when claims exceed 3% of a shipment. Look at the shipment’s claim records and available delivery information to understand whether carrier handling or delays may have contributed. Escalate the review through the Fresh Grocery Logistics team so the carrier issue can be considered and followed up.

Fresh grocery can spoil if it is exposed to warm conditions or delayed in transit. Frozen items ship with dry ice and spend at most 48 hours in transit. They do not ship on Fridays, which prevents them from sitting in a depot over the weekend. These limits reduce the time frozen products are exposed to conditions that could compromise them. When spoilage occurs despite these controls, a timely claim with a photo gives the team useful evidence to assess the issue and address the customer’s needs. The customer chooses between a refund and a new shipment. The team also reviews carrier performance when claims exceed 3% of a shipment, so recurring problems can be identified and addressed. Follow the steps below for every relevant shipment and spoilage claim.

excerpts.title: Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

Check the product and its supporting information before the livestream introduction. Confirm that the on-screen details match the product being sold, including allergen information, origin details where required, and any organic claim. For shipment, check the best-before date on the food itself. These checks cover separate risks: a correct on-screen description does not confirm the date on the stock that will ship, and a suitable date does not make an incomplete product description acceptable. If a required detail is missing, unclear, or unsupported, pause the introduction or shipment until the Fresh Grocery Quality team has advised what to do.

1. Confirm allergens are shown on screen when the product is introduced.
2. Check the best-before date on the product selected for shipment.
3. Confirm country of origin for meat and seafood, and verify the certificate number for any organic claim.
4. Hold the item if a check fails, and ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team for guidance.

Allergens such as nuts and shellfish must be shown on screen when the product is introduced. Customers may need this information before deciding whether to buy, so the relevant allergen details should be visible at the point the product is presented, not left for customers to infer from the product name or a later discussion. Check that the on-screen information corresponds to the item being introduced. If the details are missing or do not match the product, do not proceed with the introduction until the information has been checked and corrected.

For chilled food, the product must have at least 10 days left before its best-before date when it ships. For dry goods, it must have at least 90 days left before its best-before date when it ships. Check the date on the actual product selected for the order, since stock may have different dates even when it is the same item. If the product does not meet the applicable requirement, do not ship it. Ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team to confirm the next step.

The country of origin must be stated for meat and seafood. Any organic claim must include the certificate number. Confirm that these details are available and apply to the product being sold; do not add an origin or organic statement based on assumption alone.

question: What triggers a Level 2 complaint escalation, and who takes over?
answer_points: Unresolved after 24 hours or the customer threatens a public review.
A team lead takes over.
answer: A Level 2 escalation is triggered if the complaint remains unresolved after 24 hours or the customer threatens a public review, even if 24 hours have not passed. A team lead takes over. [1]

excerpts.title: Customer Complaint Escalation
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Customer Complaint Escalation > Procedure

1. Log every complaint. a. Record each complaint in the CRM and include its complaint ID. b. Add the customer’s concern, relevant communications and actions taken. Keep the record factual and update it as the complaint progresses.
2. Handle Level 1 complaints. a. A support agent must answer the complaint within 4 hours. b. The agent should acknowledge the concern, clarify any information needed, and explain the next action. The agent remains responsible for the complaint unless it meets a higher escalation level.
3. Escalate to Level 2 when required. a. A team lead takes over if the complaint is unresolved after 24 hours. b. A team lead also takes over if the customer threatens a public review, whether or not 24 hours have passed. c. The team lead reviews the CRM record, coordinates the response, and keeps the customer informed until the complaint is resolved or escalated again.
4. Escalate to Level 3 when required. a. Trust & Safety and Legal take over for any complaint involving an injury, a product safety issue or a regulator’s inquiry. b. Notify both teams promptly and provide the CRM record and relevant supporting information. Do not make commitments or speculate about responsibility while those teams review the matter. c. Continue to preserve related communications and follow the direction of Trust & Safety and Legal.
5. Keep compensation private. a. Compensation is never discussed in public comments. Discuss it only in a private message. b. If a customer raises compensation in a public comment, acknowledge the concern without discussing compensation and invite the customer to continue by private message.

excerpts.title: Account Restriction Handling
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Account Restriction Handling > Procedure

1. Identify the rule and the account: Log in to the platform's seller center and note the exact policy that was triggered, when it happened, and which livestream or product is involved. Take screenshots as evidence.
2. Check whether we caused it: Review the stream for prohibited claims, misleading product descriptions or signs of fake orders. If the cause is on our side, fix it first and appeal afterwards.
3. Collect appeal evidence: The stream recording around the flagged moment (5 minutes before and after), product certificates and shipping records. The more specific the evidence, the higher the chance the appeal succeeds.
4. Submit the appeal ticket: File a ticket in the seller center with the evidence from step 3, the account ID, the livestream ID and what we are asking for.
5. Notify the Trust & Safety contact: After filing, mention the on-call contact in the Trust & Safety channel and say how urgent it is (whether today's livestream is affected).
6. Wait for the review: It usually takes 1-3 business days. Do not file the same ticket again; duplicates push it further back in the queue.
7. Follow up on the result:
   - Appeal approved: confirm every feature is restored, save screenshots and add the case to the department knowledge base.
   - Appeal rejected: ask the Trust & Safety contact for the exact reason and decide whether to escalate to the Trust & Safety lead.

Refund and Return Requests > Procedure

1. Check the item and request. a. Confirm the delivery date and whether the item is within the 30-day return window. Customers can return an item within 30 days of delivery. b. Perishable food cannot be returned unless it arrived spoiled. For a spoiled item, follow the Fresh Grocery spoilage claim process. c. Record a reason code for every request. excerpts.title: Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval > Procedure

1. Determine the discount and applicable approver before setting or advertising a promotional price. a. A discount of up to 15% requires approval from the department manager. b. A discount between 15% and 30% requires approval from the Pricing team. c. A discount above 30% requires approval from the finance director. d. Obtain the required approval before communicating or applying the promotional price.
2. Check the proposed promotional price against the product’s cost price. a. No promotional price may go below the product’s cost price. b. Do not apply or advertise a price that fails this check.
3. Apply the approval rules to bundles. a. Assess a bundle discount as the combined discount of the bundle, not as a discount per item. b. Route the combined discount to the approver required for that discount.
4. Lock prices ahead of each stream. a. Prices are locked 24 hours before a stream. b. After the lock, make no price change without approval from the Pricing team. c. Obtain that approval before changing or communicating the revised price.
5. Keep a record of pricing decisions. a. Record the proposed price, discount, relevant product or bundle, approver, and approval. b. Make the record available to the Pricing team when requested.

Livestream Incident Response > Procedure

1. Respond to a dropped stream. a. The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes of the stream dropping. b. While the producer switches streams, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update.
2. Respond to a wrong price on screen. a. Remove the product link at once. b. Review orders placed at the wrong price. Honor orders if the error is less than 30% off the right price. Otherwise, cancel the orders and provide an apology coupon of $10. c. The host should give a brief, accurate update and avoid confirming an order outcome before it is reviewed.
3. Respond to a product that sells out mid-stream. a. The host announces that the product has sold out and moves to the next product. b. Do not promise a waitlist on air.
4. Respond to a raid of offensive comments. a. The moderator turns on slow mode and blocks the accounts posting offensive comments. b. The host does not respond to the comments and continues the stream.
5. Document and follow up. a. The responsible Live Operations staff member files the incident log within 1 hour after the stream ends. b. Send a short post-incident note the next day. Include a concise summary of what happened and the actions taken.

SOP | All departments
Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval > Purpose

This policy sets the approval requirements for promotional prices and discounts across every department. It applies to all products and bundles sold through company livestreams.

excerpts.title: Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval > Procedure

1. Determine the discount and applicable approver before setting or advertising a promotional price. a. A discount of up to 15% requires approval from the department manager. b. A discount between 15% and 30% requires approval from the Pricing team. c. A discount above 30% requires approval from the finance director. d. Obtain the required approval before communicating or applying the promotional price.
2. Check the proposed promotional price against the product’s cost price. a. No promotional price may go below the product’s cost price. b. Do not apply or advertise a price that fails this check.
3. Apply the approval rules to bundles. a. Assess a bundle discount as the combined discount of the bundle, not as a discount per item. b. Route the combined discount to the approver required for that discount.
4. Lock prices ahead of each stream. a. Prices are locked 24 hours before a stream. b. After the lock, make no price change without approval from the Pricing team. c. Obtain that approval before changing or communicating the revised price.
5. Keep a record of pricing decisions. a. Record the proposed price, discount, relevant product or bundle, approver, and approval. b. Make the record available to the Pricing team when requested.

excerpts.title: Account Restriction Handling
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Account Restriction Handling > Procedure

1. Identify the rule and the account: Log in to the platform's seller center and note the exact policy that was triggered, when it happened, and which livestream or product is involved. Take screenshots as evidence.
2. Check whether we caused it: Review the stream for prohibited claims, misleading product descriptions or signs of fake orders. If the cause is on our side, fix it first and appeal afterwards.
3. Collect appeal evidence: The stream recording around the flagged moment (5 minutes before and after), product certificates and shipping records. The more specific the evidence, the higher the chance the appeal succeeds.
4. Submit the appeal ticket: File a ticket in the seller center with the evidence from step 3, the account ID, the livestream ID and what we are asking for.
5. Notify the Trust & Safety contact: After filing, mention the on-call contact in the Trust & Safety channel and say how urgent it is (whether today's livestream is affected).
6. Wait for the review: It usually takes 1-3 business days. Do not file the same ticket again; duplicates push it further back in the queue.
7. Follow up on the result:
   - Appeal approved: confirm every feature is restored, save screenshots and add the case to the department knowledge base.
   - Appeal rejected: ask the Trust & Safety contact for the exact reason and decide whether to escalate to the Trust & Safety lead.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Consumer Electronics)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Consumer Electronics
Sale Event Inventory Check (Consumer Electronics) > Procedure

1. Identify sale inventory: Confirm the products and batches allocated to the stream with the inventory record and the warehouse team. Keep any unconfirmed stock out of the sale allocation until its status is clear.
2. Verify units and serial numbers: a. Scan every unit’s serial number and match the scan to the product and batch record. b. Resolve missing, unreadable, duplicate, or mismatched serial numbers before marking a unit as available. c. Record exceptions and keep affected units separate from sale-ready inventory.
3. Confirm firmware consistency: Check the firmware version on the units for each product. All units of a product must run the same firmware version. If versions differ, hold the affected units and coordinate with the responsible team to bring the product’s units to a consistent version before release.
4. Review batch quality history: Check the defect rate for the previous batch of each product. If the previous batch had a defect rate above 2%, hold the current batch for inspection. Do not release that batch for the stream until the inspection is complete and its disposition is recorded.
5. Check air-shipping restrictions: Identify power banks in the sale inventory and confirm their watt-hour rating. Power banks above 100 Wh can’t ship by air. Flag those units for an appropriate shipping plan and do not assign them to air transport.
6. Record the release decision: a. Mark each product and batch as approved, held, or requiring follow-up. b. Record serial-number exceptions, firmware issues, inspection holds, and shipping restrictions with the relevant inventory record. c. Share unresolved issues with the partner teams responsible for action. Release only inventory that has passed the applicable checks.
7. Closing notes: Keep the check record with the sale-event inventory documentation. Update it when a hold is cleared or an exception is resolved, and notify the stream operations team of any inventory that remains unavailable.

question: What does the Food Safety Labeling Check require staff to do before a product is introduced or released for shipping?
answer_points: Allergens such as nuts and shellfish are shown on screen when the product is introduced
Chilled food has at least 10 days left before its best-before date when it ships, and dry goods at least 90 days
The country of origin is stated for meat and seafood, and an organic claim needs its certificate number
If a check fails, the item is held and the Fresh Grocery Quality team is asked
answer:
Before introducing a product, confirm its on-screen details match the item, including allergen information, country of origin for meat and seafood, and the certificate number for any organic claim. Before shipping, check the best-before date on the actual unit selected: at least 10 days remaining for chilled food and 90 days for dry goods. [2]

If a check fails or information is missing, unclear, or unsupported, hold the introduction or shipment and ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team for guidance before proceeding. [2][3]

excerpts.title: Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery) > Purpose

Owner: Fresh Grocery Quality team. Category: Compliance.

This procedure helps Fresh Grocery staff check that product information shown during a livestream is clear and supported before an item is offered for sale. Customers use these details to decide whether a food is suitable for them and when it can be used. Missing allergen information can expose customers to ingredients they need to avoid, while an unsupported origin or organic claim can mislead them about what they are buying. Date checks also help prevent food from shipping too close to its best-before date. The check applies to product information on screen and to the product prepared for shipment. Staff should resolve gaps before the product is introduced or released for shipping, rather than relying on a correction after a customer has placed an order.

excerpts.title: Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

Check the product and its supporting information before the livestream introduction. Confirm that the on-screen details match the product being sold, including allergen information, origin details where required, and any organic claim. For shipment, check the best-before date on the food itself. These checks cover separate risks: a correct on-screen description does not confirm the date on the stock that will ship, and a suitable date does not make an incomplete product description acceptable. If a required detail is missing, unclear, or unsupported, pause the introduction or shipment until the Fresh Grocery Quality team has advised what to do.

1. Confirm allergens are shown on screen when the product is introduced.
2. Check the best-before date on the product selected for shipment.
3. Confirm country of origin for meat and seafood, and verify the certificate number for any organic claim.
4. Hold the item if a check fails, and ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team for guidance.

Allergens such as nuts and shellfish must be shown on screen when the product is introduced. Customers may need this information before deciding whether to buy, so the relevant allergen details should be visible at the point the product is presented, not left for customers to infer from the product name or a later discussion. Check that the on-screen information corresponds to the item being introduced. If the details are missing or do not match the product, do not proceed with the introduction until the information has been checked and corrected.

For chilled food, the product must have at least 10 days left before its best-before date when it ships. For dry goods, it must have at least 90 days left before its best-before date when it ships. Check the date on the actual product selected for the order, since stock may have different dates even when it is the same item. If the product does not meet the applicable requirement, do not ship it. Ask the Fresh Grocery Quality team to confirm the next step.

The country of origin must be stated for meat and seafood. Any organic claim must include the certificate number. Confirm that these details are available and apply to the product being sold; do not add an origin or organic statement based on assumption alone.

excerpts.title: Food Safety Labeling Check (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:

excerpts.content:

Staff can also overlook the different remaining-date requirements for chilled food and dry goods, omit the country of origin for meat or seafood, or use an organic claim without its certificate number. If information is absent or does not match the product, do not guess or leave the issue for the customer to resolve.

question: What are the partner teams' responsibilities in the Home Goods Sale Event Inventory Check?
answer_points: Warehouse & Logistics confirms space for bulky items, supports stock checks, and helps resolve inventory or carton damage issues.
Livestream Operations confirms the event forecast and product plan and reviews inventory exceptions affecting the stream.
Home Goods Supply Chain owns the inventory check, coordinates resolutions, and confirms event stock is ready.
answer: Warehouse & Logistics confirms space for bulky items, supports stock checks, and helps resolve inventory or carton damage issues. Livestream Operations confirms the event forecast and product plan and reviews inventory exceptions that could affect the stream. The Home Goods Supply Chain team owns the inventory check, coordinates resolutions, and confirms when event stock is ready. [1]

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Home Goods
Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods) > Partner Teams

- Warehouse & Logistics: Confirm warehouse space for bulky items, support stock checks, and help resolve inventory or carton damage issues.
- Livestream Operations: Confirm the event forecast and product plan, and review any inventory exceptions that could affect the stream.
- Home Goods Supply Chain team: Own the inventory check, coordinate resolutions, and confirm when event stock is ready.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Home Goods
Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods) > Procedure

1. Review the forecast: Confirm the expected demand for each product with the event team. Keep stock 10% above the forecast to provide a buffer for livestream orders.
2. Confirm available stock: Compare the forecast and buffer with inventory records. Flag any shortage or mismatch for review before the event stock is reserved.
   - For a multi-pack, count the pack as a single SKU.
   - Confirm that each product’s stock is available for the event and not already committed elsewhere.
3. Check bulky-item space: Confirm warehouse space for every bulky item in the event. Do not treat an item as ready until the warehouse confirms the space is available.
4. Inspect cartons: Open 5% of cartons and check the contents for damage. Record any damage and flag affected stock so it is not treated as ready for the stream.
5. Resolve exceptions: Review shortages, stock mismatches, damage, and space concerns with the relevant partner teams. Confirm the resolution before finalizing the event inventory.
6. Reserve event stock: Once checks are complete, reserve the approved event stock in the inventory system. Share any remaining exceptions with the event team so they can adjust the product plan.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Home Goods
Sale Event Inventory Check (Home Goods) > Procedure

1. Review the forecast: Confirm the expected demand for each product with the event team. Keep stock 10% above the forecast to provide a buffer for livestream orders.
2. Confirm available stock: Compare the forecast and buffer with inventory records. Flag any shortage or mismatch for review before the event stock is reserved.
   - For a multi-pack, count the pack as a single SKU.
   - Confirm that each product’s stock is available for the event and not already committed elsewhere.
3. Check bulky-item space: Confirm warehouse space for every bulky item in the event. Do not treat an item as ready until the warehouse confirms the space is available.
4. Inspect cartons: Open 5% of cartons and check the contents for damage. Record any damage and flag affected stock so it is not treated as ready for the stream.
5. Resolve exceptions: Review shortages, stock mismatches, damage, and space concerns with the relevant partner teams. Confirm the resolution before finalizing the event inventory.
6. Reserve event stock: Once checks are complete, reserve the approved event stock in the inventory system. Share any remaining exceptions with the event team so they can adjust the product plan.

Promotional price — The price offered during a promotion or livestream.

excerpts.title: Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval > Procedure

1. Determine the discount and applicable approver before setting or advertising a promotional price. a. A discount of up to 15% requires approval from the department manager. b. A discount between 15% and 30% requires approval from the Pricing team. c. A discount above 30% requires approval from the finance director. d. Obtain the required approval before communicating or applying the promotional price.
2. Check the proposed promotional price against the product’s cost price. a. No promotional price may go below the product’s cost price. b. Do not apply or advertise a price that fails this check.
3. Apply the approval rules to bundles. a. Assess a bundle discount as the combined discount of the bundle, not as a discount per item. b. Route the combined discount to the approver required for that discount.
4. Lock prices ahead of each stream. a. Prices are locked 24 hours before a stream. b. After the lock, make no price change without approval from the Pricing team. c. Obtain that approval before changing or communicating the revised price.
5. Keep a record of pricing decisions. a. Record the proposed price, discount, relevant product or bundle, approver, and approval. b. Make the record available to the Pricing team when requested.

excerpts.title: Customer Complaint Escalation
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Customer Complaint Escalation > Purpose

This policy sets the escalation process for customer complaints across every department. The Customer Service team owns the process and is responsible for maintaining a complete complaint record.

excerpts.title: Customer Complaint Escalation
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Customer Complaint Escalation > Procedure

1. Log every complaint. a. Record each complaint in the CRM and include its complaint ID. b. Add the customer’s concern, relevant communications and actions taken. Keep the record factual and update it as the complaint progresses.
2. Handle Level 1 complaints. a. A support agent must answer the complaint within 4 hours. b. The agent should acknowledge the concern, clarify any information needed, and explain the next action. The agent remains responsible for the complaint unless it meets a higher escalation level.
3. Escalate to Level 2 when required. a. A team lead takes over if the complaint is unresolved after 24 hours. b. A team lead also takes over if the customer threatens a public review, whether or not 24 hours have passed. c. The team lead reviews the CRM record, coordinates the response, and keeps the customer informed until the complaint is resolved or escalated again.
4. Escalate to Level 3 when required. a. Trust & Safety and Legal take over for any complaint involving an injury, a product safety issue or a regulator’s inquiry. b. Notify both teams promptly and provide the CRM record and relevant supporting information. Do not make commitments or speculate about responsibility while those teams review the matter. c. Continue to preserve related communications and follow the direction of Trust & Safety and Legal.
5. Keep compensation private. a. Compensation is never discussed in public comments. Discuss it only in a private message. b. If a customer raises compensation in a public comment, acknowledge the concern without discussing compensation and invite the customer to continue by private message.

excerpts.title: Post-Livestream Review Process (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Post-Livestream Review Process (Beauty) > Procedure

1. Pull the core numbers: GMV, DAU, average watch time and conversion rate, compared with the same period of the previous campaign in the category.
2. Break it down by hour: Look at the hourly traffic curve, mark the hours with unusually high or low conversion, and replay the host's script and product lineup at those times.
3. Analyze by product: Which SKUs drove most of the GMV, which ones were listed but never converted, and whether to keep scheduling them.
4. Analyze by host: Compare lead capture and conversion with the host's historical average to judge whether this was a normal performance.
5. Log incidents: Record any platform restrictions, equipment failures or complaints, how long they took to resolve and what they affected, and pass them to the team that owns the matching SOP.
6. Hold the review meeting: The data team prepares a one-page summary; host, ops and supply chain meet for 30 minutes and agree on 2-3 concrete improvements for next time.
7. Archive: Store the review document in the department's shared library, tagged with the campaign_id, so the next similar campaign can find it.

excerpts.title: Campaign Review Writing Guidelines
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Campaign Review Writing Guidelines > Steps

1. Pull figures from the uploaded data tables; never estimate numbers by hand.
2. Compare each result with its target range: inside the range is on target, below it is below target, above it is above target.
3. Calculate ROI as total product profit divided by actual operating cost.
4. Use product profit after cost of goods; do not subtract cost of goods again.
5. Compare actual operating cost with the plan.
6. If operating cost is more than 5% over plan, flag it in bold and explain the overage.
7. Write the product breakdown from the uploaded data tables.
8. Add recommendations for similar campaigns, based on the results and cost review.
9. Check that every required section is present before sharing the review.

answer: The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes; while that happens, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update. [1]

excerpts.title: Livestream Incident Response
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Livestream Incident Response > Procedure

1. Respond to a dropped stream. a. The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes of the stream dropping. b. While the producer switches streams, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update.
2. Respond to a wrong price on screen. a. Remove the product link at once. b. Review orders placed at the wrong price. Honor orders if the error is less than 30% off the right price. Otherwise, cancel the orders and provide an apology coupon of $10. c. The host should give a brief, accurate update and avoid confirming an order outcome before it is reviewed.
3. Respond to a product that sells out mid-stream. a. The host announces that the product has sold out and moves to the next product. b. Do not promise a waitlist on air.
4. Respond to a raid of offensive comments. a. The moderator turns on slow mode and blocks the accounts posting offensive comments. b. The host does not respond to the comments and continues the stream.
5. Document and follow up. a. The responsible Live Operations staff member files the incident log within 1 hour after the stream ends. b. Send a short post-incident note the next day. Include a concise summary of what happened and the actions taken.

heading_path: Product Demo Setup for Livestreams (Consumer Electronics)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Consumer Electronics
Product Demo Setup for Livestreams (Consumer Electronics) > Procedure

1. Select and prepare demo units. a. Confirm the product matches the livestream plan and is in working condition. b. Ensure all demo units are fully charged and running the latest firmware before the stream. c. Set up a backup unit for every product that is demonstrated. Confirm it is charged, functional, and ready to use.
2. Prepare the demonstration area. a. Place each product and its accessories within the host’s reach. b. Keep cables and other equipment organized so they do not obstruct the host or appear as a safety hazard. c. Confirm products are clean and positioned so viewers can see relevant features.
3. Test connectivity and presentation. a. Test screen mirroring 30 minutes before the stream. Confirm the correct device is connected and its display is visible in the stream. b. Check that any required connections, controls, and demonstration content work as intended. c. If screen mirroring or another essential function fails, troubleshoot before the stream. Use the backup unit when appropriate and notify the production lead if the issue remains unresolved.
4. Conduct product demonstrations. a. Demonstrate product features accurately and follow the livestream plan. b. Hosts never compare the product with a competitor’s by name. Keep comparisons focused on the product’s own features and intended use. c. Demonstrate earbuds and speakers below 85 dB. Monitor the sound level during the demonstration and lower it if it reaches the limit. d. Do not continue a demonstration if the product becomes unsafe, stops working, or cannot be presented accurately. Switch to the backup unit or inform the production lead.
5. Complete the setup check. a. Confirm the demo unit and backup unit are ready and accessible. b. Confirm the host understands the demonstration plan and the requirements in this procedure. c. Report unresolved equipment or setup issues to the production lead before the stream begins.

excerpts.title: Refund and Return Requests
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Refund and Return Requests > Procedure

1. Check the item and request. a. Confirm the delivery date and whether the item is within the 30-day return window. Customers can return an item within 30 days of delivery. b. Perishable food cannot be returned unless it arrived spoiled. For a spoiled item, follow the Fresh Grocery spoilage claim process. c. Record a reason code for every request. Use one of these codes: wrong item, damaged, changed mind or quality issue.
2. Review the request and determine the refund amount. a. For an item bought at a livestream-only price, calculate the refund using the price the customer paid, not the list price. b. If the refund is above $500, obtain sign-off from a Customer Service team lead before issuing it.
3. Process the return and refund. a. Provide the customer with the applicable return instructions and track the returned item. b. Issue the refund within 5 business days after the returned item is received. c. Record the outcome and any required approval in the order record.

excerpts.title: Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Promotional Pricing and Discount Approval > Procedure

1. Determine the discount and applicable approver before setting or advertising a promotional price. a. A discount of up to 15% requires approval from the department manager. b. A discount between 15% and 30% requires approval from the Pricing team. c. A discount above 30% requires approval from the finance director. d. Obtain the required approval before communicating or applying the promotional price.
2. Check the proposed promotional price against the product’s cost price. a. No promotional price may go below the product’s cost price. b. Do not apply or advertise a price that fails this check.
3. Apply the approval rules to bundles. a. Assess a bundle discount as the combined discount of the bundle, not as a discount per item. b. Route the combined discount to the approver required for that discount.
4. Lock prices ahead of each stream. a. Prices are locked 24 hours before a stream. b. After the lock, make no price change without approval from the Pricing team. c. Obtain that approval before changing or communicating the revised price.
5. Keep a record of pricing decisions. a. Record the proposed price, discount, relevant product or bundle, approver, and approval. b. Make the record available to the Pricing team when requested.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > When to Use

Use this procedure before every Beauty sale stream. The check is done 72 hours before the stream so the team has time to resolve stock, shelf-life, shade availability, and storage issues before products are presented to customers. Beauty inventory needs a product-level review: a total count can look adequate while specific lipstick or foundation shades are short, expired stock can be mixed with eligible stock, and testers or free samples can make sellable quantities appear higher than they are. The review also confirms that temperature-sensitive serums are stored correctly. These checks protect customers from products with too little shelf life, prevent unavailable shades from being offered, and give the stream team a reliable view of what it can sell. The Beauty category manager signs off the check after the required reviews are complete.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > Procedure

1. Review timing and scope: Start the check 72 hours before the stream. Confirm the sale list and review every product planned for sale. This timing gives the team a clear point to identify issues and coordinate any changes before the stream.
2. Check shelf life: Confirm the remaining shelf life for each product. Do not put any product with less than 6 months of shelf life left on sale. This rule keeps products with insufficient remaining shelf life out of the offer and reduces the risk of customer complaints.
3. Check shade-level stock: Review lipstick and foundation inventory shade by shade. Take a shade with fewer than 50 units out of the stream. A product-level total does not show whether each shade can support the offer, so each shade needs its own decision.
4. Separate sellable stock: Count testers and free samples separately from sellable stock. Do not include them in the quantity available for sale. This keeps the sale quantity accurate and prevents non-sellable items from being treated as customer inventory.
5. Confirm storage and sign-off: Check that temperature-sensitive serums are stored below 25°C. Record any issue for resolution before the stream, then send the completed check to the Beauty category manager for sign-off. Correct storage helps protect serum quality, and manager sign-off confirms that the inventory review is complete.

excerpts.title: Campaign Review Writing Guidelines
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Campaign Review Writing Guidelines > Steps

1. Pull figures from the uploaded data tables; never estimate numbers by hand.
2. Compare each result with its target range: inside the range is on target, below it is below target, above it is above target.
3. Calculate ROI as total product profit divided by actual operating cost.
4. Use product profit after cost of goods; do not subtract cost of goods again.
5. Compare actual operating cost with the plan.
6. If operating cost is more than 5% over plan, flag it in bold and explain the overage.
7. Write the product breakdown from the uploaded data tables.
8. Add recommendations for similar campaigns, based on the results and cost review.
9. Check that every required section is present before sharing the review.

Findings:

1. Power Bank led on units, sales, profit, and margin. It sold 3,481 units for $282.2K in sales and $124.0K in profit, with a 43.94% margin.
2. Bluetooth Speaker had the highest return rate at 19.4%. Its $279.2K in sales came with a 33.79% margin and $94.3K in profit. Check return reasons before using it as a lead product again.
3. Wireless Earbuds had the lowest return rate at 1.9%, but the fewest units and lowest sales. It sold 745 units for $143.0K in sales and $43.9K in profit, with a 30.72% margin.
4. Operating cost exceeded the plan while all three campaign performance targets were met. This supports reviewing cost controls separately from product and audience performance.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > How It Works

1. Check that frozen items are packed with dry ice and scheduled to spend at most 48 hours in transit.
2. Do not ship frozen items on Fridays; this avoids weekend depot delays.
3. If a customer reports spoilage, request a claim within 24 hours of delivery and ask for a photo.
4. Offer the customer a choice between a refund and a new shipment.
5. If claims exceed 3% of a shipment, review the carrier.

Keep the claim process straightforward. Use the delivery time to determine whether the claim was made within 24 hours, and make sure the photo is attached to the claim record. The photo helps the team understand the reported condition instead of relying only on a description. Record the customer’s chosen resolution and route the case through the normal fulfillment process.

The shipping rules are preventive controls, not a guarantee that spoilage cannot occur. Dry ice supports frozen products during transit, while the transit limit and Friday restriction reduce exposure to delays. If a shipment misses its expected timing or arrives with a problem, handle the customer’s report under the claim process rather than assuming the packaging controls were sufficient.

Review the carrier when claims exceed 3% of a shipment. Look at the shipment’s claim records and available delivery information to understand whether carrier handling or delays may have contributed. Escalate the review through the Fresh Grocery Logistics team so the carrier issue can be considered and followed up.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > Purpose

Owner: Fresh Grocery Logistics team. Category: Fulfillment.

Fresh grocery can spoil if it is exposed to warm conditions or delayed in transit. This procedure sets clear shipping and claim rules so customers receive safe products and the team can respond consistently when a shipment arrives spoiled. Frozen items ship with dry ice and spend at most 48 hours in transit. They do not ship on Fridays, which prevents them from sitting in a depot over the weekend. These limits reduce the time frozen products are exposed to conditions that could compromise them. When spoilage occurs despite these controls, a timely claim with a photo gives the team useful evidence to assess the issue and address the customer’s needs. The customer chooses between a refund and a new shipment. The team also reviews carrier performance when claims exceed 3% of a shipment, so recurring problems can be identified and addressed. Follow the steps below for every relevant shipment and spoilage claim.

excerpts.title: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
heading_path: Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Cold Chain Shipping and Spoilage Claims (Fresh Grocery) > Common Mistakes

Do not schedule frozen items to ship on Fridays. A shipment can then remain at a depot over the weekend, increasing the risk of spoilage.

Do not omit dry ice or allow frozen items to spend more than 48 hours in transit.

Do not treat a spoilage report as a complete claim without a photo, or overlook the requirement that the claim be made within 24 hours of delivery.

Do not choose the resolution for the customer. The customer decides between a refund and a new shipment.

Do not ignore the carrier review threshold. When claims exceed 3% of a shipment, start a carrier review.

excerpts.title: Refund and Return Requests
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Refund and Return Requests > Procedure

1. Check the item and request. a. Confirm the delivery date and whether the item is within the 30-day return window. Customers can return an item within 30 days of delivery. b. Perishable food cannot be returned unless it arrived spoiled. For a spoiled item, follow the Fresh Grocery spoilage claim process. c. Record a reason code for every request. Use one of these codes: wrong item, damaged, changed mind or quality issue.
2. Review the request and determine the refund amount. a. For an item bought at a livestream-only price, calculate the refund using the price the customer paid, not the list price. b. If the refund is above $500, obtain sign-off from a Customer Service team lead before issuing it.
3. Process the return and refund. a. Provide the customer with the applicable return instructions and track the returned item. b. Issue the refund within 5 business days after the returned item is received. c. Record the outcome and any required approval in the order record.
4. Direct livestream questions to the order page. a. Hosts and moderators must never promise a refund in the live chat. b. Hosts and moderators must point the customer to the order page to submit or follow up on a request.

excerpts.title: Account Restriction Handling
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Account Restriction Handling > Procedure

1. Identify the rule and the account: Log in to the platform's seller center and note the exact policy that was triggered, when it happened, and which livestream or product is involved. Take screenshots as evidence.
2. Check whether we caused it: Review the stream for prohibited claims, misleading product descriptions or signs of fake orders. If the cause is on our side, fix it first and appeal afterwards.
3. Collect appeal evidence: The stream recording around the flagged moment (5 minutes before and after), product certificates and shipping records. The more specific the evidence, the higher the chance the appeal succeeds.
4. Submit the appeal ticket: File a ticket in the seller center with the evidence from step 3, the account ID, the livestream ID and what we are asking for.
5. Notify the Trust & Safety contact: After filing, mention the on-call contact in the Trust & Safety channel and say how urgent it is (whether today's livestream is affected).
6. Wait for the review: It usually takes 1-3 business days. Do not file the same ticket again; duplicates push it further back in the queue.
7. Follow up on the result:
   - Appeal approved: confirm every feature is restored, save screenshots and add the case to the department knowledge base.
   - Appeal rejected: ask the Trust & Safety contact for the exact reason and decide whether to escalate to the Trust & Safety lead.

excerpts.title: Livestream Incident Response
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Livestream Incident Response > Procedure

1. Respond to a dropped stream. a. The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes of the stream dropping. b. While the producer switches streams, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update.
2. Respond to a wrong price on screen. a. Remove the product link at once. b. Review orders placed at the wrong price. Honor orders if the error is less than 30% off the right price. Otherwise, cancel the orders and provide an apology coupon of $10. c. The host should give a brief, accurate update and avoid confirming an order outcome before it is reviewed.
3. Respond to a product that sells out mid-stream. a. The host announces that the product has sold out and moves to the next product. b. Do not promise a waitlist on air.
4. Respond to a raid of offensive comments. a. The moderator turns on slow mode and blocks the accounts posting offensive comments. b. The host does not respond to the comments and continues the stream.
5. Document and follow up. a. The responsible Live Operations staff member files the incident log within 1 hour after the stream ends. b. Send a short post-incident note the next day. Include a concise summary of what happened and the actions taken.

excerpts.title: Post-Livestream Review Process (Fresh Grocery)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Fresh Grocery
Post-Livestream Review Process (Fresh Grocery) > Procedure

1. Prepare the core numbers: The Fresh Grocery Data team prepares the spoilage complaint rate and the sell-through of each perishable product. Use these measures to identify customer concerns and understand which products sold through and which remain. Looking at every perishable product separately helps the team avoid hiding a problem with one item inside an overall result.
2. Review customer feedback and the stream: Discuss spoilage complaints in the context of what customers saw and heard during the livestream. The host explains how products were presented and responds to any questions about what happened on air. This discussion helps distinguish issues with product condition from issues with how the product or its handling was explained.
3. Review product sell-through: Go through sell-through for each perishable product with the supply chain planner. Identify products with stock left over and discuss what affected their sale, including relevant supply or availability context. Product-level review gives the team a clear basis for handling remaining stock rather than relying on a general impression of the stream.
4. Agree on stock actions: Move perishable stock left over to other channels within 24 hours. Agree on the next channel and the handoff needed to make the move. The time limit exists because perishable stock can lose value or become unsuitable for sale if action is delayed.
5. Record the review: The Fresh Grocery Data team records the core numbers, the main discussion points, and the agreed stock actions. A clear record lets the department follow through on decisions and refer to the review when preparing future livestreams.

New Campaign Launch Checklist > Procedure

1. Set up the campaign in the system: Enter the campaign name, owning department, category, start and end dates and budget in the ops console.

3. Verify product compliance: Every product in the campaign has its certificates in place (beauty and food products need the relevant permits), and every product link can be ordered.
4. Check coupons and prices: Discounts, stock levels and prices match the product pages, so there is no pricing incident on air.
5. Test the streaming setup: Test the network, equipment and lighting one hour before going live, so the stream does not start with a technical failure.
6. Look at past results: Check GMV, DAU and conversion rate of similar past campaigns and judge whether this campaign's targets are realistic.
7. Run a policy self-check: Go through the host script against the Trust & Safety list of restricted phrases, so the stream is not throttled right at the start.
8. Confirm the contingency plan: Know whom to call for an equipment failure, a network outage or a platform restriction (see the matching SOPs).

excerpts.title: Black Friday Readiness Checklist 2025
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Black Friday Readiness Checklist 2025 > Procedure

1. Confirm advertising budgets. a. Each department must confirm that its advertising budget is approved by October 31, 2025. b. The responsible team must share confirmation with the Ops team. Raise any outstanding approval as a readiness risk.
2. Finalize the stream schedule. a. The stream schedule must be final by November 7, 2025. b. Departments involved in programming, staffing, or stream operations must confirm their commitments against the final schedule.
3. Freeze inventory. a. Inventory is frozen on November 14, 2025. b. No stock moves between warehouses after that date. c. Teams responsible for inventory and fulfilment must plan warehouse stock needs before the freeze and follow the restriction during Black Friday operations.
4. Load test checkout. a. The checkout is load tested on November 18, 2025. b. The teams responsible for checkout and technical operations must review the test results and raise any issue that could affect purchases with the Ops team.
5. Prepare studio backup equipment. a. New in 2025: a second backup stream encoder is required for every studio. b. Studio and stream operations teams must confirm that each studio has the encoder available and ready for use before Black Friday.
6. Staff the war room. a. The war room must be staffed from 8 am to midnight during Black Friday week. b. The Ops team must coordinate coverage with every department. Each department must identify the appropriate contact for readiness questions and live issues, and ensure that contact knows how to reach the war room.

excerpts.title: Livestream Incident Response
excerpts.content:
SOP | All departments
Livestream Incident Response > Procedure

1. Respond to a dropped stream. a. The producer switches to the backup stream within 2 minutes of the stream dropping. b. While the producer switches streams, the host keeps talking and gives viewers a brief update.
2. Respond to a wrong price on screen. a. Remove the product link at once. b. Review orders placed at the wrong price. Honor orders if the error is less than 30% off the right price. Otherwise, cancel the orders and provide an apology coupon of $10. c. The host should give a brief, accurate update and avoid confirming an order outcome before it is reviewed.
3. Respond to a product that sells out mid-stream. a. The host announces that the product has sold out and moves to the next product. b. Do not promise a waitlist on air.
4. Respond to a raid of offensive comments. a. The moderator turns on slow mode and blocks the accounts posting offensive comments. b. The host does not respond to the comments and continues the stream.
5. Document and follow up. a. The responsible Live Operations staff member files the incident log within 1 hour after the stream ends. b. Send a short post-incident note the next day. Include a concise summary of what happened and the actions taken.

excerpts.title: Host Onboarding and Review (Home Goods)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Home Goods
Host Onboarding and Review (Home Goods) > Procedure

1. Prepare the host: Explain the Home Goods product range, livestream expectations, and how the onboarding and review process works. Confirm the host knows where to find product information and whom to contact with questions.
2. Practise product demos: Have the new host practise clear, accurate demonstrations of Home Goods products. Practice should include assembling storage bins and using a spin mop. Review how the host explains product features and answers viewer questions.
3. Run trial streams: Schedule 2 trial streams of 90 minutes each. Review each stream for product knowledge, demonstration quality, audience engagement, and ability to handle questions. Share feedback after each stream and identify any areas the host should improve.
4. Review performance: Compare the host's average order value with the department average. Discuss the results with the host alongside feedback on product demonstrations and viewer interactions. Agree on practical steps to address any gaps.
5. Manage probation: Probation lasts 90 days. During probation, review the host's performance and provide coaching on any identified issues. At the end of probation, assess the review results and determine whether the host is ready to continue hosting for Home Goods.
6. Record the outcome: Document trial-stream feedback, the average order value comparison, coaching, and the probation decision in the host's record. Share relevant next steps with the host and the teams supporting their work.

excerpts.title: Post-Livestream Review Process (Home Goods)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Home Goods
Post-Livestream Review Process (Home Goods) > Procedure

1. Prepare the review: Gather the records for the streams from the week before. Check that the host and merchandiser can attend, and share the material they will need to discuss the results.
2. Review the core numbers: Look at average order value, bundle attach rate and damage-in-transit complaints. Use these numbers to focus the discussion on order value, product combinations and delivery damage. Note any questions that need follow-up.
3. Discuss the stream together: Review the week’s streams as a group rather than treating each stream as a separate review. Ask the host and merchandiser to share what they observed, including which product presentations or bundles worked well and where customers had concerns.
4. Record findings and follow-up: Capture the key observations, the core numbers and any agreed actions in the review record. Assign each action to the team or person responsible, and note what information is still needed.
   - If damage-in-transit complaints came up, record the relevant issue and pass it to the team that can investigate delivery or packaging.
   - If the discussion identifies a product or bundle question, record the details for the merchandiser to follow up.
   - If the host identifies a presentation issue, record it for the appropriate host support team.
5. Share and retain the review: Send the summary and follow-up actions to the people involved. Keep the record with the Home Goods review materials so the team can refer to it in later weekly discussions.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > Procedure

1. Review timing and scope: Start the check 72 hours before the stream. Confirm the sale list and review every product planned for sale. This timing gives the team a clear point to identify issues and coordinate any changes before the stream.
2. Check shelf life: Confirm the remaining shelf life for each product. Do not put any product with less than 6 months of shelf life left on sale. This rule keeps products with insufficient remaining shelf life out of the offer and reduces the risk of customer complaints.
3. Check shade-level stock: Review lipstick and foundation inventory shade by shade. Take a shade with fewer than 50 units out of the stream. A product-level total does not show whether each shade can support the offer, so each shade needs its own decision.
4. Separate sellable stock: Count testers and free samples separately from sellable stock. Do not include them in the quantity available for sale. This keeps the sale quantity accurate and prevents non-sellable items from being treated as customer inventory.
5. Confirm storage and sign-off: Check that temperature-sensitive serums are stored below 25°C. Record any issue for resolution before the stream, then send the completed check to the Beauty category manager for sign-off. Correct storage helps protect serum quality, and manager sign-off confirms that the inventory review is complete.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > When to Use

Use this procedure before every Beauty sale stream. The check is done 72 hours before the stream so the team has time to resolve stock, shelf-life, shade availability, and storage issues before products are presented to customers. Beauty inventory needs a product-level review: a total count can look adequate while specific lipstick or foundation shades are short, expired stock can be mixed with eligible stock, and testers or free samples can make sellable quantities appear higher than they are. The review also confirms that temperature-sensitive serums are stored correctly. These checks protect customers from products with too little shelf life, prevent unavailable shades from being offered, and give the stream team a reliable view of what it can sell. The Beauty category manager signs off the check after the required reviews are complete.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > When to Use

Use this procedure before every Beauty sale stream. The check is done 72 hours before the stream so the team has time to resolve stock, shelf-life, shade availability, and storage issues before products are presented to customers. Beauty inventory needs a product-level review: a total count can look adequate while specific lipstick or foundation shades are short, expired stock can be mixed with eligible stock, and testers or free samples can make sellable quantities appear higher than they are. The review also confirms that temperature-sensitive serums are stored correctly. These checks protect customers from products with too little shelf life, prevent unavailable shades from being offered, and give the stream team a reliable view of what it can sell. The Beauty category manager signs off the check after the required reviews are complete.

excerpts.title: Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty)
excerpts.content:
SOP | Beauty
Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > Procedure

1. Review timing and scope: Start the check 72 hours before the stream. Confirm the sale list and review every product planned for sale. This timing gives the team a clear point to identify issues and coordinate any changes before the stream.
2. Check shelf life: Confirm the remaining shelf life for each product. Do not put any product with less than 6 months of shelf life left on sale. This rule keeps products with insufficient remaining shelf life out of the offer and reduces the risk of customer complaints.
3. Check shade-level stock: Review lipstick and foundation inventory shade by shade. Take a shade with fewer than 50 units out of the stream. A product-level total does not show whether each shade can support the offer, so each shade needs its own decision.
4. Separate sellable stock: Count testers and free samples separately from sellable stock. Do not include them in the quantity available for sale. This keeps the sale quantity accurate and prevents non-sellable items from being treated as customer inventory.
5. Confirm storage and sign-off: Check that temperature-sensitive serums are stored below 25°C. Record any issue for resolution before the stream, then send the completed check to the Beauty category manager for sign-off. Correct storage helps protect serum quality, and manager sign-off confirms that the inventory review is complete.

excerpts.content:

Sale Event Inventory Check (Beauty) > Partner Teams

- Beauty Supply Chain team: Owns the check, reviews sale inventory, and coordinates resolution of inventory issues.
- Warehouse & Logistics: Confirms stock counts, separates testers and free samples from sellable stock, and verifies serum storage conditions.
- Beauty category manager: Reviews and signs off the completed check.
- Livestream operations team: Updates the stream plan when a shade or product is removed from the sale.
